title: Why does my child spell words the way they sound?
meta_description: Children spell by sound because early spelling starts there. What the national curriculum expects in Years 1 and 2, what to correct, and what can wait.
keywords: spell words the way they sound
hero_image_alt: A closed navy exercise book, a sharpened pencil, a pencil sharpener and a mug of tea beside a blank ruled notepad on a pale wooden table.
content_html:
A child who spells words the way they sound is doing what early spelling is built on: turning the sounds they hear into letters. The national curriculum for England expects Year 1 and Year 2 pupils to make phonically plausible attempts, and says misspellings of words already taught should be corrected. A sound based attempt is a sensible first try, not carelessness.

Key takeaways

  • Early spelling starts from sounds, and the national curriculum notes for Year 1 and Year 2 expect some words to be spelled in a phonically plausible way even when the spelling is not standard.
  • The curriculum guidance is to correct misspellings of words a child has been taught, and to use other misspelt words to teach alternative ways of writing the same sounds.
  • English often has more than one spelling for a sound, so a sound based attempt can be sensible and still wrong. Silent letters, spellings that no longer match speech, and accent all add to this.
  • The expectation changes across primary school. By Years 3 and 4 the curriculum says spelling of common words should be correct, and in Years 5 and 6 children are expected to draw on how words are built.

Why does my child spell words the way they sound?

Children spell by sound because writing a word starts with hearing its sounds and choosing letters for them. The national curriculum describes this as a process: a pupil breaks a spoken word into its separate sounds (phonemes), then writes a letter or letters (graphemes) for each one in the right order.

Take a child who writes "sed" for "said". The first half of the job is done well. Every sound is there, in order, and each has a letter that could plausibly stand for it. The second half is choosing which of the possible spellings is the standard one, and that part has to be learnt word by word.

The spelling appendix to the curriculum puts the underlying difficulty in one sentence: "Most people read words more accurately than they spell them." Reading asks a child to recognise a spelling. Spelling asks the child to produce one, and where a sound can be written several ways, the sound alone does not say which.

What does the national curriculum say about spelling by sound?

The national curriculum treats sound based spelling as expected in Year 1 and Year 2, and it gives a clear instruction about correction. The statutory requirements for Year 1 say pupils should be taught to spell words containing each of the forty or more phonemes already taught, and to spell common exception words.

The notes that sit alongside those requirements are marked as guidance rather than law, and they are more specific about what children actually do:

  • The Year 1 notes say that at this stage pupils will be spelling some words in a phonically plausible way, even if sometimes incorrectly.
  • The Year 2 notes say children’s spelling should be phonically plausible, even if not always correct.
  • Both years say misspellings of words that pupils have been taught to spell should be corrected. On what to do with the rest, the wording differs slightly: the Year 1 notes say other misspelt words should be used to teach pupils about alternative ways of representing those sounds, and the Year 2 notes say they can be used as an opportunity to do so.

The Year 1 introduction, which sits above those notes, also says pupils’ writing during that year will generally develop at a slower pace than their reading, because they have to encode the sounds they hear in words. That is a description of the task, not a verdict on any one child.

Why does spelling by sound go wrong in English?

Spelling by sound goes wrong in English because the link between sounds and letters is not one to one. The curriculum and its spelling appendix name several reasons, summarised here.

What a child hearsWhat can go wrongWhat the curriculum says
One sound that can be written in more than one wayThe child picks a plausible spelling that is not the standard oneThe Year 2 introduction says the same sound can be spelt in different ways
A word with a letter that is not soundedThe child leaves the letter outThe Year 2 introduction refers to so called silent letters
A word spoken in the child’s own accentThe sounds the child hears may differ from the ones the spelling reflectsThe appendix says some words are exceptions in some accents but not in others, and gives past, last, fast, path and bath as examples

The Year 2 introduction also describes spelling that has become separated from the way words are now pronounced, using the "le" ending in "table" as its example. For the longer history of why this happens, the post on why English spelling is so hard to learn goes through it.

The appendix adds that phonic knowledge should continue to underpin spelling after Key Stage 1, but that pupils also increasingly need to understand morphology (how words are built from parts) and etymology (where words come from). The post on prefixes and suffixes covers the first of those.

Is it a problem if my child keeps spelling this way?

In Year 1 and Year 2, sound based spelling is not a problem in itself, because the curriculum notes expect it. The expectation moves on as children get older. The Years 3 and 4 introduction says pupils’ spelling of common words should be correct, including common exception words and other words they have learnt. The Years 5 and 6 introduction says spelling of most words taught so far should be accurate, and the statutory requirements for those years include using knowledge of morphology and etymology in spelling.

A child in the upper years of primary school who still writes almost every word by sound alone is working below that pattern, but one example in a birthday card does not show how widespread it is. The class teacher is the person who can say what the school is working on and which words are being taught.

What should I correct, and what can wait?

The curriculum’s guidance is to correct misspellings of words a child has been taught, and to treat other misspelt words as a chance to teach another way of writing a sound. That is guidance written for teachers, and it says nothing about what a parent should do at home.

Read plainly, it suggests a simple rule for a family. Words from the school spelling list are the ones that have been taught, so a wrong spelling of one of those is worth correcting. In free writing, such as a card or a diary entry, a spelling that is sensible but not standard can be a prompt for one short comment, for example that the sound is written another way in this word. Correcting every word in a piece of free writing is not something the curriculum guidance asks for.

How can a child learn the standard spelling of a word?

A child learns the standard spelling of a taught word by paying attention to the part that does not match the sound. The spelling appendix says teachers should draw pupils’ attention to the grapheme phoneme correspondences that do and do not fit what has been taught, which is the same idea in classroom language.

Look, cover, write, check is the method schools use for this. The child looks at the word, covers it, writes it from memory, then checks it against the original. The checking step is where a sound based attempt becomes useful, because a child can see exactly which letters differ from the standard spelling, and that is usually one or two. This reasoning comes from how the method works, not from a study. The page on look, cover, write, check explains each step, and how spelling sticks covers why a word needs to be written from memory on more than one day.

What does research say about early invented spelling?

Researchers use the term invented spelling for the nonstandard spelling children produce when they write words by their sounds. A study by Darlene Tangel and Benita Blachman followed children into first grade after a period of kindergarten instruction in phoneme awareness, which means hearing and separating the sounds in spoken words. The children who had received it significantly outperformed the comparison children on measures of both invented and standard spelling.

Frequently asked questions

What is a phonically plausible spelling?

A phonically plausible spelling is one that could represent the sounds of a word even though it is not the standard spelling. The national curriculum introduction to Year 2 says pupils should be able to make phonically plausible attempts to spell words they have not yet learnt.

Does spelling by sound mean my child needs more phonics?

Not by itself. The Year 1 introduction says pupils who are still struggling to decode and spell need to be taught to do this urgently through a rigorous and systematic phonics programme. A sound based attempt at a tricky word is not the same thing as struggling to decode, and the class teacher is the person to ask about which applies.

Does my child’s accent matter for spelling?

It can. The spelling appendix says some words are exceptions in some accents but not in others, and gives past, last, fast, path and bath as examples. Spelling is learnt word by word, so the standard spelling is the same whatever the accent.

By what age should spelling be accurate?

The curriculum does not set a single age. Its Years 3 and 4 introduction says spelling of common words should be correct, and its Years 5 and 6 introduction says spelling of most words taught so far should be accurate.
